📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout.

Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?

Industry observers note that as Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.

Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Sources indicate that shares in the frontier AI tech giant behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.

Sources indicate that anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.

US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.

It has been revealed that neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, remarked there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”.

Sources indicate that global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.

Sources indicate that in Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.

It has been revealed that european stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.

The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, remarked Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.

“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp noted.

Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, remarked: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

In a recent development, “The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, uber has opened its ride-hailing service to children as young as 10 in three U.S.
  • The program, which builds on Uber’s existing teen ride-hailing service for passengers ages 13 to 17, is the latest bid by Uber to expand its customer base.
  • The Uber Kids program is stacked with mandatory requirements for parents and drivers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, uber has opened its ride-hailing service to children as young as 10 in three U.S. cities as the company tests whether there’s a market for shuttling tweens without an adult by their side. The program, called Uber Kids, launched quietly over the past few weeks in Austin, Texas, Nashville, Tennessee, and Madison, Wisconsin.

The program, which builds on Uber’s existing teen ride-hailing service for passengers ages 13 to 17, is the latest bid by Uber to expand its customer base. Uber is describing this as a limited pilot program, which means it may never expand beyond these cities or even exist by next year. But if successful, it could open up a potentially lucrative market for Uber: busy families with active kids.

The Uber Kids program is stacked with mandatory requirements for parents and drivers. Parents or guardians are the only ones who can order a ride for their child, which they can do by adding the child to their family profile and completing a mandatory onboarding that explains the built-in safety features. A parent or guardian must be present at the pickup locations for the trip to begin and also have to include a note to the driver that explains the drop off.

In a recent development, meanwhile, only highly rated drivers who have been invited are allowed to participate. Those drivers are required to complete an education module that includes step-by-step instructions and must be opted into live video streaming so parents can watch the trip in real time, according to Uber.

Uber remarked it also requires PIN verification for every Uber Kids trip, and says all recordings will be encrypted and not available to the driver, and will use sensors and GPS data to detect if the ride goes off course, stops unexpectedly, or ends early.

Drivers who are willing to adhere to those rules to shuttle kids will get a pay bump for the effort, according to Uber. Eligible drivers will earn $7 more on every Uber Kids trip compared to a standard one, the organization states on the dedicated Uber Kids web page. Drivers will receive an extra $20 for the first Uber Kids ride they complete.

It has been revealed that the extra compensation underscores a key challenge Uber faces as it expands into this younger age group — how to convince drivers to take on that added responsibility. If the program does expand it could eventually compete with existing transportation services such as HopSkipDrive and Zum.

Recent findings suggest that uber opened its ride-hailing service to minors in 2023 when it launched Uber for Teens, although the company had conducted early pilots several years prior. As the program expanded nationwide, Uber introduced a live video streaming feature.

#47295. Watching as a giant star swallowed its neighbor and exploded

Watching as a giant star swallowed its neighbor and exploded

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion.
  • In a new Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025.
  • Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion. The process, known as common envelope evolution, was proposed in the 1970s to explain how some of the tightest pairs of stars in the Universe form, but no one had ever caught it in the act.

In a new Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025. “It lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” Karambelkar noted. “Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it’s really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.”.

Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk. Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for that shrinkage. When one star in a binary grows old, it expands into a giant, and its outer layers can engulf its companion. The two then share a single, loosely bound envelope of gas. As the engulfed star drags through it, it loses orbital energy to friction and spirals inward. Depending on how much of the envelope gets lost, the pair either ends up in a much tighter orbit or merges.

According to recent reports, karambelkar’s team spotted a candidate system where this might be happening while searching Andromeda for stars changing in brightness, using the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) telescope at Palomar Observatory and data from NASA’s Near-Earth Object Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (NEOWISE) mission. One giant had been brightening for seven years. “When a star first swallows its companion, it has a very subtle effect on its brightness,” Karambelkar mentioned. “It slowly brightens, and a lot of light comes out in the infrared.”.

Recent findings suggest that in April 2025, Karambelkar’s team published a paper suggesting that this system, named AT 2025abao, was undergoing an engulfment in progress. Back then, though, they couldn’t rule out a competing explanation: a single star with instabilities deep within its core. So, they kept watching.

In a recent development, the researchers reconstructed the history of the system using observations from about a dozen telescopes and surveys, going back to photographic sky plates from 1989. Until 2018, the star barely changed. Modeling those quiet years revealed a giant late in its life, about 350 times wider than the Sun. Its companion was impossible to see, however. “The giant star outshines the smaller star by a factor of about 18,000,” Karambelkar said.

Recent findings suggest that to get around it, the team estimated the mass of the smaller companion based on the amount of dust the system had shed before the engulfment. The estimates suggested a star of roughly 0.7 solar masses.

Between 2018 and early 2025, the giant brightened two- to threefold in visible light, swelling while its temperature stayed nearly constant. Karambelkar compares the process to a spacecraft reentering Earth’s atmosphere. The companion, skimming through the giant’s outer layers, was gradually seeing its orbit shrink, and the friction was heating up the envelope. The energy released by that drag matched the extra light the team observed.

Then, the star’s visible light dropped by half while its infrared glow kept rising. NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope happened to catch it in July 2025, revealing that the giant had swollen to some 860 times the Sun’s width and wrapped itself in fresh dust.

In a recent development, in October 2025, the star brightened roughly 100-fold in just 25 days, shining like 1.5 million Suns at its peak. “At one point, the rate at which the orbit was decaying became very, very fast,” Karambelkar stated, comparing the release of the gravitational energy to an explosion. “The companion just fell very promptly, very deep inside the envelope of the star, and it crashed into the core. That violent crash set off a bomb inside the star, and that explosion caused it to brighten very quickly and eject some of the material.”.

The eruption had all the hallmarks of a luminous red nova, a type of outburst known to come from merging stars—but an event the researchers weren’t expecting. “Honestly, our minds were blown,” Karambelkar noted. He said that this was evidence that this explosion was a consequence of the inspiraling of a binary companion. What made AT 2025abao special, though, was the giant itself.

It has been revealed that all previously known luminous red novae came from younger stars with dense, tightly bound outer layers, which inevitably drive both stars toward a merger. This one was an old giant with a loose, churning envelope—the setup that can also leave behind a surviving tight binary. To find out if the companion actually survived, the team looked at how AT 2025abao’s energy was spent.

To predict how such events end, astronomers use a formula with an efficiency parameter describing how much of the energy lost by the sinking companion goes into blowing the envelope away. AT 2025abao revealed that the energy goes to different places at different stages.

According to recent reports, during the slow spiral, most of the energy escaped as light. In the final plunge, the companion released about a hundred times more energy, but only around 1 percent of it was radiated away. Nearly all the rest went into hurling a tenth of the envelope outward at about 10 times the speed needed to escape the giant’s gravity. The rest of the envelope stayed put, which suggests the companion merged with the giant’s core instead of surviving as a tight partner.

It has been revealed that “Initially, when the rate of energy deposition is low, the star is able to puff up and adjust to this newly introduced energy source inside it,” Karambelkar stated. “But once the energy deposition rate increases very promptly as the companion spirals even closer, the star can no longer adjust itself. At that point, it needs to throw out some of its material.”.

Industry observers note that the efficiency the team calculated fits values inferred from known post-engulfment binaries. But the formula assumes the energy is mostly spent expelling lots of the envelope. Here, most of it went into flinging a small amount of gas at high speeds. It turned out the formula works as a rule of thumb but misses some of the physics.

In AT 2025abao, gas shed during the slow spiral piled up in the plane of the binary’s orbit, so the explosion’s ejecta could expand freely toward the poles even though it was blocked around the equator. That, Karambelkar argues, explains the hourglass-shaped nebulae seen around dying stars. “It had been an idea for a very long time that those hourglass shapes are shaped by binary interactions,” he stated. “It seems like what we’re seeing here confirms that hypothesis.”.

Recent findings suggest that the team admits it can’t yet be sure the stars merged, because dust formed from the ejected material hides whatever is left inside. “We want to continue monitoring the system for several years, possibly even decades, to watch the dust clear out and whatever is remaining inside emerge,” Karambelkar said. “That will conclusively tell us whether this merged or the binary system survived.” In the meantime, the team hopes to find many more such events involving stars of different masses and types.

In a recent development, telescopes we have today can detect them only as far as Andromeda, but the Vera Rubin Observatory and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope should spot them in about 100 Milky Way-like galaxies within some 50 million light-years. “We can have an influx of several of these events per year,” Karambelkar mentioned.

Nature, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11221-z.

Germany seems to be serious about a TikTok Europe takeover

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Donald Trump-backed proposal that resulted in a US-led takeover of TikTok's American business has apparently inspired some leaders in the European Union.
  • It has been revealed that "It's a pan-European initiative and we think that they are able to invest around about 25 billion euros in that kind of business," Berlin culture minister Wolfram Weimer told the outlet.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you're thinking, "wait, I didn't know TikTok Europe was for sale," that's because...
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The tech giant has called the idea “nonsense.”.

The Donald Trump-backed proposal that resulted in a US-led takeover of TikTok's American business has apparently inspired some leaders in the European Union. This week Germany and Austria proposed a similar move for the app's European operation, and now the German government states that it has lined up investors willing to fork over as much as €25 billion (about $27.4 billion USD) to finance such an arrangement, Politico reports.

It has been revealed that "It's a pan-European initiative and we think that they are able to invest around about 25 billion euros in that kind of business," Berlin culture minister Wolfram Weimer told the outlet. "And TikTok Europe should be open to sell 75% to 80% of the shares." Investors from five countries have expressed interest in such a deal, according to Weimer.

Recent findings suggest that if you're thinking, "wait, I didn't know TikTok Europe was for sale," that's because... it isn't. At least not in any official sense. And unsurprisingly, it doesn't seem like ByteDance is at all interested in this arrangement, which a spokesperson has described as "nonsense." Of course, TikTok's US business wasn't officially for sale either. But we all know how that ended.

According to recent reports, whether a similar EU-led takeover of TikTok would actually gain any traction is unclear. The app isn't facing a ban in the region. And, as Bloomberg, pointed out earlier this week, Germany and Austria likely can't strongarm the company into a sale without the backing of the whole European Commission.

It has been revealed that EU officials have raised similar concerns as their US counterparts about TikTok's influence and its ties to China. Last year, the EU fined the organization more than $600 million for breaking EU privacy laws by funneling some EU user data to China. More recently, regulators have accused the company of breaking its Digital Services Act (DSA) with its "For You" algorithm. The EU Commission has told the company to change the design of its algorithm or it risks another massive fine.

Breaking: Germany news: Kids take to streets over school, climate and costs

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Below, you can review a roundup of the biggest headlines in Germany from Friday, November 20:.
  • Representatives of IG Metall, Germany's largest union, mentioned Friday that thousands of union workers at dozens of factories around the country will continue to carry out 24-hour strikes in an effort to force employers to cough up a 5% wage increase as well as job guarantees.
  • Audi, BMW, Ford, Opel and Volkswagen are all in IG Metall's sights, as are shipyards in northern Germany.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This blog is now closed. Thank you for reading.

Below, you can review a roundup of the biggest headlines in Germany from Friday, November 20:.

Representatives of IG Metall, Germany's largest union, mentioned Friday that thousands of union workers at dozens of factories around the country will continue to carry out 24-hour strikes in an effort to force employers to cough up a 5% wage increase as well as job guarantees.

Audi, BMW, Ford, Opel and Volkswagen are all in IG Metall's sights, as are shipyards in northern Germany.

Companies say they cannot afford to pay wage increases and will have to slash benefits, site upgrades and hundreds of thousands of jobs in the automotive, electrical and mechanical engineering and metal production sectors.

They are instead offering a phased increase of 1.3% for 2028 — Germany's current inflation rate is hovering around 3%.

It is the first time the union and its 3.7 million members have turned to 24-hour strikes in eight years and they are hoping the move will offer them some leverage when collective bargaining talks begin next week.

In a recent development, IG Metall's northern coastal representative Daniel Friedrich stated Friday: "Our members stand united behind our demands. On Monday, we will continue the 24-hour strikes at more companies.".

Police in the German state of Saxony say they deployed water cannons to Leipzig and used them on individuals who repeatedly shot fireworks at officers there after a large demonstration ended.

Police say roughly 2,500 people took part in a demonstration in Leipzig organized by the group Gen Z Takes Charge, far fewer than the estimated 7,000 who joined the first of these on October 31 (see entries below).

Across Germany, some 87,000 people joined in demonstrations, according to Gen Z Takes Charge.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday confirmed that Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani had pledged €15 billion ($16.5 billion) in newly introduced German defense and technology investments.

During a Berlin press conference with the emir, Merz noted, "This strengthens both of us, particularly in future technologies such as artificial intelligence, semiconductors and aviation.".

The Qatar-Germany collaboration is aimed at improving security and defense projects that also include defending against cyberattacks, with Merz saying, "We are particularly open to newly introduced partnerships in the defense industry.".

That cooperation comes as both nations look to beef up defenses amid regional conflicts with global consequences.

The chancellor and the emir also stressed the fundamental importance of diplomacy in the resolution of conflict, with the two leaders' focused largely on Iran and the Middle East — and the need to get the flow of shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz closer to pre-war levels.

The emir called for deescalation, saying, "We are convinced that true political resolution is the only way to achieve lasting peace.".

In a recent development, merz added that the two agreed on the war in Ukraine, saying: "Russia must stop its time-wasting diplomatic games. Moscow has to finally sit down for real peace negotiations.".

Merz was straightforward on Iran, saying Germany wants peace in the Middle East because it needs affordable energy.

He later called out Russian maritime marauding on the Black Sea, labeling it a threat to global food security.

The German broadcaster Sky TV — not to be confused with the British-based Sky Sports F1 which is the largest English-language commercial F1 broadcaster — will not be sending any staff to the Formula 1 Qatar Grand Prix because of security concerns in connection with the conflict in Iran and the wider Middle East.

Sky TV declared the move on Friday, just a week before the contentious race weekend from November 27-29.

Sky will broadcast the entire race weekend as usual, but will use global feed images and will not send any of its own staff to Lusail International Circuit.

F1 races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia this spring were canceled as the US war with Iran was in its most active phase, with major disruptions to commercial flights.

The season-ending double header in Qatar and then the United Arab Emirates a week later has been in serious doubt ever since.

Nominally at least, both races are going ahead — and in all likelihood, teams will have already started dispatching equipment and personnel to the region to begin preparations by now.

Sky TV remarked it still planned to send a team to the season finale in Abu Dhabi, just across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, on December 6.

But it noted it continued to "monitor developments and assess the situation on an ongoing basis.".

Organizers of the Gen Z Takes Charge protest group spoke out about why they took to the streets again.

Co-organizer Akram Selo called on Germany's leadership to meet the young people's demands.

"Talks won't make us stop demonstrating," he told RBB-Inforadio in comments aired on Friday.

Sources indicate that "Essentially, our demands should be addressed, and we should be given assurances. That is what needs to happen, not empty promises," Selo added.

"So far, we feel that we aren't being taken seriously at all," he remarked. "The way we're being treated suggests that the aim is to sideline our demands and discriminate against us by focusing on other trivial matters.".

Another group, the alliance "School strike against conscription" held its own protest to demand an immediate halt to surveys about potential availability for the German Armed Forces, or Bundeswehr, that are currently non-binding and only obligatory for teenage boys.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz mentioned Ukraine must ‌continue ⁠to ⁠push ahead swiftly with reforms, particularly ​on the rule of ​law and tackling ​corruption, ‌if it hopes to receive a prerequisite for further financial ‌aid and investment.

Merz made the comment at a ‌business ​summit in Berlin that was organized by the German Chamber of Industry and Commerce.

"It is now essential to press ahead with these reforms swiftly and resolutely —particularly, and I say this openly, with regard to the rule of law and corruption," Merz told attendees.

The German chancellor said that sustained reform efforts by Kyiv ​were necessary to justify long-term Western support ⁠for ​Ukraine, adding ​that Germany would ​step up ‌its backing in defense and humanitarian ​aid ⁠as Russia intensifies attacks on ⁠Ukraine's ​energy infrastructure ahead of winter.

"What we invest in Ukraine now, we will receive back many times over as dividends in the form of stability, export opportunities, joint projects, and growth," the German chancellor stated.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In 2025, the two countries traded goods worth around €12 billion ($13 billion).

Industry observers note that "Freedom and security are now unleashing forces of progress and resilience on a scale never seen before. This is precisely the stance we are now taking against the autocratic and imperialist actors of this world. We are the world of freedom," Merz added.

In a recent development, at home, Merz has faced increasing pressure to justify Germany's ongoing support for Ukraine. In recent regional elections, political parties opposing sending military aid have performed well.

Merz argued that Russia's war against Ukraine is an attack on democratic values everywhere.

Germany's electricity exports rose in the first three quarters of this year, according to official data released on Friday.

According to the energy association BDEW, Germany has been a net importer of electricity since 2023.

The neighbouring countries Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands, were the most important buyers of German electricity in the first nine months of 2026.

Together, they bought about half of all German electricity exports.

Recent findings suggest that the volume of German electricity exported rose by 25.5% compared with the same period last year, to 48.8 terawatt-hours, while its value increased by 51.3% to €4.3 billion ($4.7 billion). Electricity imports into Germany fell by 13.3% in volume, but at 49.2 terawatt-hours they remained slightly above exports.

While imported electricity cost an average of €116 per megawatt-hour, 39% more than a year earlier, exported electricity from Germany averaged only €87 per megawatt-hour, some 20.6% more than a year earlier.

With a high share of renewable energy sources, wind and solar, Germany tends to offer electricity when supply is high and prices are low, but in times of shortage it has to pay higher prices for imported electricity.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Finance Ministry officials mentioned they are launching a dialogue process, dubbed "Germany 2035," to develop proposals for the future of the country's economy.

Officials want to study how Germany can secure growth and prosperity and what that could look like in terms of fiscal policy.

Finance Minister Lars ​Klingbeil will begin the dialogue process on December ​2, when he welcomes economists from around the world to Berlin.

Additionally, think tanks, research organizations, universities and civil society groups have been asked to host workshops, which would take place in the first half of 2027.

Among 12 economic topics that the ministry seeks to explore are tax and fiscal policy, investment ⁠and ​domestic demand, industrial policy, energy ​and climate transition, foreign trade and sovereignty, and housing ​and local infrastructure.

The dialogue will culminate in a white paper, to be published in 2028, that can provide recommendations for Germany's economic future up to 2035.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

A group called "Gen Z Takes Charge" (Gen Z regelt) has called for thousands of young people to demonstrate in many German cities.

The gathering comes almost three weeks after the first major youth protests hit Germany, inspired by the protests that took place in France in the last weeks.

Those protests, which took place on October 31, saw tens of thousands take to the streets across Germany, with crowds remaining largely peaceful, although rioting broke out in several cities, including Frankfurt, later in the evening.

Among the demands of the "Gen Z Takes Charge" group are increased funding for schools, addiction support and psychotherapy, affordable living, opposition to conscription and consistent action on climate change.

Another group, the Federal Pupils' Conference, has also organized its own demonstration at the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin, with police saying that some 5,000 people have already signed up.

The pupils' conference advocates for improvements in education policy in Germany, including school renovation, school social work, relief for teachers and the inclusion of climate action in curricula.

The demonstrations are set to begin in the morning and run until late afternoon.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier welcomed the Emir of Qatar Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani in Berlin with military honors.

Steinmeier will also host a state banquet for the emir and his delegation in the evening. Al Thani is also expected to meet with Chancellor Friedrich Merz during the day.

The visit comes in the midst of tensions in the Middle East, with the war in Iran likely to be a critical topic in the talks between the two governments. Qatar is at the moment one of the mediators in the deadlocked conflict between the US and Iran.

Economic and bilateral relations are also expected to take center stage.

On Saturday, the emir will visit Germany's most populous state of North Rhine-Westphalia, where he will be greeted by its state premier Hendrik Wüst at the military section of Cologne/Bonn Konrad Adenauer Airport.

During the visit, Al Thani and North Rhine-Wesphalia leaders will hold an economic conference in the small city of Königswinter, near Bonn, where the Emir will also visit Drachenburg Castle.

Following a political summit on Ukraine in Berlin yesterday, the German Chamber of Industry and Commerce (DIHK) mentioned it would host a German-Ukrainian business forum.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz and German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche are expected to be in attendance, along with Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi, among others.

Christian Bruch, deputy chair of the Eastern Committee of the German Economy and chief executive of Siemens Energy, mentioned German companies are committed to invest in Ukraine, despite Russia's ongoing war and were open to expand their business partnerships.

Bruch mentioned bilateral trade was expected to rise to around €13 billion ($14.1 billion) in 2026.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

German flagship airline Lufthansa looks to cut 1,000 jobs at its airport hubs in Frankfurt and Munich, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.

The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa Airlines CEO Jens Ritter and four other managers.

Industry observers note that the timeframe of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were apart of a previously unveiled downsizing.

In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.

Lufthansa's parent manufacturer Lufthansa Group had 67,100 employees in Germany by the end of last year. In the letter seen by news agencies, Lufthansa said financial struggles were the reason behind the planned cuts.

"Lufthansa is presently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said, while pointing out that the firm operated at a €180 million ($197 million) loss in the first nine months of this year.

In addition, Lufthansa Airlines is now in its third straight year of being unprofitable.

In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.

Leaked documents raise latest questions about Deutsche Bank's dealings in Russia up to Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, adding to scrutiny over the bank's risk controls and past controversies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and notes he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi.

Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.

In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also mentioned he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.

Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.

At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.

It has been revealed that “We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.

He remarked Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.

Sources indicate that “You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.

“We want them to build it here.”.

With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.

The Trump administration on Monday issued fresh rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it mentioned was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.

China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.

In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and mentioned: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”.

He added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”.

Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.

Industry observers note that “I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president said. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”.

Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran.

“I can’t speak to America,” he stated, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.”.

He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election.

“I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said.

Trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He said Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.”.

In a recent development, and he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”.

These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s going down, as the American rapper Yung Joc might say: the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms.
  • Sources indicate that apple Pay went down.
  • The first thought, naturally, is an AI hacker invasion of some sort, especially after hackers managed to attack fridges in a grocery store and a blood bank in France a few weeks ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s going down, as the American rapper Yung Joc might say: the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms. In the past two weeks, the U.S.’s top businesses have faced technical outages that have disrupted the systems that run everyday life.

Sources indicate that apple Pay went down. NASA’s internal communication network went down. The FAA had to ground all flights for hours (only the third time in history since 9/11), and Microsoft was hit with an outage that took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for nearly two days.

The first thought, naturally, is an AI hacker invasion of some sort, especially after hackers managed to attack fridges in a grocery store and a blood bank in France a few weeks ago. Here in the U.S., the director of National Intelligence mentioned these outages don’t seem related to state-sponsored terrorism, while President Trump called the issues “individual events.” Many of the companies themselves have said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks or AI attacks, but tech issues.

Only, there’s the fact that they all struck within a short timespan of each other, and just a few weeks after Cybersecurity’s so-called “Black October,” when a slew of also-unrelated cybersecurity incidents occurred on October 21, striking PHP, Node.js, LiteLLM, more.

While there’s no reason to view these outages as cyberattacks, there may be more than coincidence going on: It’s giving AI-native Y2K, frankly.

Dave DeWalt, an investor who worked in cybersecurity for more than three decades (including as president and CEO of McAfee and as vice chairman of the CISA Advisory Council for the Department of Homeland Security), also thinks it’s probably AI-related.

The technical outages are most likely the “growing pains of a security system that’s getting stronger, not weaker,” and that “AI is surfacing vulnerabilities at a speed and scale we’ve never had before through AI tools like Mythos and others,” he told TechCrunch.

Industry observers note that the thing is, many of these technical flaws have always existed, but because AI is surfacing them so fast, enterprises are rushing to fix them before bad actors can exploit them. “That surge in patching is disrupting things in the short term,” he said.

This was, perhaps, the first moment when legacy meets modern, Anusha Iyer, a software engineer and founder of the security startup Corsha, told TechCrunch. “These industrial systems were never designed to be connected, let alone securely connected in the way we are pushing them to be today,” she said.

Virginia Senator Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intel Committee, came to a similar conclusion (although investigations are still underway as to what could be happening). “These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” the senator wrote on X.

Industry observers note that AI is reshaping how software is built, deployed, and operated, on a scale where everyone feels the sharp learning curve. Iyer cited the FAA outage as an example of legacy tech that is not as sophisticated or advanced as the technologies companies are trying to merge it with.

In less technical terms, she mentioned the outage may have been caused (and preliminary findings point to this) when the FAA was trying to modernize its telecommunications infrastructure and the transition overwhelmed parts of its legacy hardware, where the new tech likely operated at a normal modern capacity while the legacy hardware couldn’t keep up.

When looked at this way, she remarked, AI is actually getting the bad rep. “It’s not rapid adoption of AI yet causing these outages,” she said. “The fault is the rushed mix of the legacy and modern systems without a clear understanding of operational and cyber risk or the ability to gatekeep and protect the legacy systems.”.

Organizations need a more steadfast approach to AI adoption, including more testing and prioritizing what needs to be fixed and when, DeWalt said.

Iyer added, “These industrial systems need to be segmented more tightly and more access controlled, so as modern systems are introduced, it can be phased in and risk mitigated.”.

In a recent development, actually, there might be a silver lining to all of this for companies (and for venture investors). DeWalt said he’d rather see these U.S. enterprises find and patch their flaws, even in this messy way, than have bad actors find and exploit those vulnerabilities in AI warfare that could cause even more national security challenges.

And maybe some aspiring founders were inspired by them. DeWalt expects a rise in companies focused on “AI-driven vulnerability management, autonomous remediation, safe patch testing and deployment, and resilience for the systems that keep critical infrastructure running,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that “There’s real pain in this transition as we’ve seen in the past week,” DeWalt said. “But there’s also enormous opportunity for the companies that help organizations move at AI speed without breaking things.”.

Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (925 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most important temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.
  • Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.
  • According to recent reports, the Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most important temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.

Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.

According to recent reports, the Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.

In a recent development, the east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.

For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.

But now there has been a breakthrough.

After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.

The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle.".

It has been revealed that only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.

Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.

And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.

In 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.

Then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!".

Recent findings suggest that nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go.".

The researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.

Digitally fitting the fragments together led to another vital discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.

The Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.

According to recent reports, using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most important fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.

Sources indicate that alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.

Recent findings suggest that there is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.

Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.

In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.

In the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.

Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.

Greece, however, considers them stolen.

Industry observers note that for years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.

The exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The historic launch is happening while Rockstar workers vote on union recognition.

    Sources indicate that unsurprisingly, a lot of people have bought Grand Theft Auto 6. Rockstar Games announced Friday that, based on manufacturer estimates, the open-world crime game made $3.79 billion in day-one retail sales and sold 32.5 million copies in pre-release. That last total is notably above the 20 million pre-orders some analysts expected Rockstar to sell ahead of the game's launch.

    In a recent development, "It is with immense gratitude that we enter a new chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of Grand Theft Auto VI," Sam Houser, Rockstar's president and founder, said in a statement. "We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn't be more excited to share this moment with you.".

    According to recent reports, GTA 6 has easily lapped the previous entry in the series, Grand Theft Auto 5, which made over $800 million worldwide from about 11 million units in its first day of sales in 2013. GTA 6 is more expensive, starting at $80 rather than GTA V's $60, but clearly demand has built up in the 13 years it took Rockstar to get the series' latest entry ready for launch.

    Sources indicate that after years of industry-wide layoffs, it's not clear if the game's early success will actually translate into security for Rockstar Games' workers. According to a Guardian op-ed from a Rockstar North developer, the studio's staff are worried that layoffs could happen even though the game is making money hand over fist. Rockstar workers are voting on whether they'll recognize their branch of the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain between November 12 and November 26. "We go where the team goes," Jennifer Kolbe, Rockstar's head of publishing, told Bloomberg in October. "So if they want a union, they will have a union.".

    At the same time, Rockstar has been accused of union busting. The studio laid off a group of more than 30 developers in October 2025, most of whom were trying to organize its workers. Rockstar says it terminated its former employees because they were sharing confidential information, and their case has played out in an employment tribunal in the lead-up to GTA 6's release. The result of the union vote or the tribunal could shape the studio's future just as much as its latest game being a smash hit.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey.

    A upcoming draft deal omits any mention of how to phase out fossil fuels, in what campaigners call a step 'backwards' and a 'glaring regression'.

    Like in previous years, the climate summit is likely to be extended until a consensus is reached.

    These are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20 and Saturday, November 21:.

    The UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, has gone into overtime, with countries still divided over key issues, including fossil fuels and climate financing.

    According to recent reports, the talks were scheduled to end on Friday evening, but negotiators have yet to reach an agreement. Germany and several other countries are pushing for a clear commitment to phase out fossil fuels, while poorer nations are demanding more concrete financial support to cope with climate change.

    Sources indicate that negotiations are expected to continue into the weekend. We are pausing our live coverage for now and will bring you further updates as talks progress.

    While Turkey hosts COP31 in Antalya, a growing climate threat is unfolding on its Mediterranean beaches. Rising sand temperatures are causing most newly hatched sea turtles to be born female, raising concerns about the long-term survival of local populations.

    Conservationists warn that climate change, combined with pollution, coastal development and fishing-related injuries, is putting increasing pressure on the species.

    DW correspondent Julia Hahn follows the people working to protect Turkey's iconic loggerhead turtles and indicates how the climate crisis is already affecting wildlife far beyond the COP31 conference halls.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Sources indicate that the UN climate summit in Antalya is drawing criticism from activists and campaigners who question whether global climate talks can deliver meaningful change while fossil fuel interests remain influential. Turkey and Australia, both under scrutiny for their energy policies, are leading this year's conference.

    It has been revealed that activists, including Greta Thunberg, argue COP summits have become increasingly ineffective, while others defend them as a vital space to pressure governments. Climate policy experts say the talks have helped reduce projected warming, but stress that real progress depends on action taken by countries between summits, not just agreements reached at them.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    For the Maldives, climate change is already affecting everyday life. Heavy rainfall has forced people from their homes, warmer oceans are damaging coral reefs, and changes in fish stocks are putting pressure on the country's fishing industry. Rising sea levels pose another threat to the low-lying island nation. Meanwhile, global greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise, despite more than three decades of international climate negotiations.

    At COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, the Maldives' climate minister Ali Sharif discusses why progress has been so slow, what really happens during climate negotiations, and why moving away from fossil fuels is not as straightforward as it might seem.

    For island nations like the Maldives, switching to renewable energy comes with practical and financial challenges. So what would it take to accelerate the transition? And can the UN climate process still deliver meaningful results?

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    The hosts of next year's COP, Ethiopia, found a nationally tailored sporting metaphor to sum up the difficult, ongoing, sometimes tortuous process that the global environmental meetings can prove to be.

    Speaking at the end of Friday's plenary to confirm Addis Ababa's intentions to host next year's summit, Gedion Timothewos, the foreign minister and upcoming president of COP32, made reference to Ethiopia's longstanding success in endurance running in track and field.

    Referring to the COP process as a marathon, not a sprint, Timothewos mentioned the country was looking forward to picking up the baton from Turkey and leading the next leg of the relay, taking the ongoing process forward into 2027.

    His comments came during a late-night plenary session, but more talks are still expected in Antalya.

    Shortly after 9 p.m. local time in Antalya, delegates gathered for a plenary session, well past the official closing time.

    The Turkish presidency's opening address was partly drowned out by a protester shouting objections in English such as "you are killing the future," and gaining applause within the chamber.

    According to recent reports, "We've been negotiating for days to find the common ground," COP31 President Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister, told the plenary. He hailed the progress made and noted the world "waits for good news from this room.".

    But the plenary session noted how several of the more ambitious aspects of a political declaration remained incomplete, with no agreement yet reached at the summit.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Several national delegates spoke during the plenary to bemoan the elusive progress or even backsliding during the two weeks of negotiations.

    The evening's session, however, has been dealing with technical complications, and the possibility that discussions continue into the weekend remains.

    In a recent development, attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?

    The UN's IPCC should have already started work on its next series of multi-year scientific assessments on climate change's progress, but the process is on hold at the urging of countries including fossil fuel-producing giants Russia, Saudi Arabia and Iran.

    Read Tim Schauenberg's full report on this obstruction to climate research and other similar issues complicating COP31 here.

    It has been revealed that the US government is snubbing UN climate talks in Turkey. That's prompted a delegation of American lawmakers, mayors and governors to make the trip instead, aiming to show that climate action in the US is alive and well.

    Head over to this report to learn more about who is representing the US at the summit, even if President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly dismissed global warming as a "hoax", didn't send a formal delegation for the second year in a row.

    Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.

    Learn more about what Uganda's environment minister Beatrice Atim Anywar noted about climate financing in this report.

    Veteran climate justice advocate Victor Menotti of the Demand Climate Justice NGO told DW that European governments appeared to be copying US President Donald Trump's negotiating playbook at COP this year.

    "We know the US isn't here, but we can see that Germany and other European governments have learned a few of the Trump tactics, maybe in the trade disputes with the US," Menotti remarked. "And we see them applying here in Antalya, where it's like: Don't admit to anything. Try to dilute your responsibilities. Weaken whatever obligations you have. And then take even more.".

    He argued these countries were also expecting unreasonable or unfeasible commitments from developing countries, for instance restrictions on what they can spend money on and obligations to report on their expenditures.

    "Germany is subsidizing quite a bit of coal still and fossil fuels, LNG expansion infrastructure," he stated, arguing that wealthier countries' energy spending also had room for improvement.

    Industry observers note that "We need the North to act first," Menotti mentioned. "The deal from Paris, the deal from Rio 30 years ago, is that the North will lead. But yet we see too much bullying of the global South and not enough leadership like they agreed to.".

    You can cross off another box on your COP31 bingo cards, dear readers.

    Sources indicate that as of the top of this hour, the session has officially gone past its scheduled end time of 1500 GMT/UTC on Friday, or 6 p.m. local time on site in Turkey.

    This is something of an annual tradition at COP summits, which are always scheduled to finish at the end of a working week but also almost invariably run into the closing weekend. Delegates and members of the media tend to book their travel intends with this in mind.

    The revised draft declaration, which critics have slammed as "watered down" due to the omission of fossil fuels, highlights the "electrification" of the global economy as a central pillar of the energy transition.

    "Electrification is the key to transitioning away from fossil fuels," Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen told reporters.

    What are the key points to know about the "35-by-35" electrification target?

    But the text does not specify what energy sources would supply the electricity. Some countries are demanding that the text call for "clean" electrification to clearly favor renewable sources over coal, oil or gas.

    Bowen, who has been trying to secure compromises, pledged to continue working over the "coming hours, for as long as it takes, to get the job done.".

    Industry observers note that "People have strong views of course — I am not stepping away from that. But no one has mentioned to me let's give up and go home," Bowen said.

    The Climate Action Network (CAN), a global network of over 2,500 civil society organizations, has accused wealthy developed nations, led by the EU, "of blocking every track" towards a substantive agreement on fighting climate change and curbing fossil fuel use.

    At its final press conference of the summit, CAN executive director Tasneem Essop said the group was "rejecting what is presently on the table.".

    In a recent development, "There is nothing (...) that protects people or addresses the priorities of the Global South. In fact, the opposite is true. The current text has opened the door to the most harmful and dangerous options of any COP so far," Essop noted.

    She pointed out that this year's COP had the highest ever number of lobbyists for fossil fuels, for AI, for CCUS (Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage) and for CDR (Carbon Dioxide Removal), which only represent corporate interests and do not have the interests of the people from developing nations who are most at risk from global warming in mind.

    "What we’re leaving this COP with is decisions made to promote the interests of those corporations making profits from the destruction of people," Essop said.

    In a recent development, mohamed Adow from Power Shift Africa, which is also part of CAN, said: "The COP Presidents want to tell us this has been a great COP. Well, I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever.

    "Overseeing a failing COP is bad enough, but trying to sell it as a success rubs salt into the wounds of those people who need it to deliver.".

    Adow cautioned that communities that live with the constant threat of drought, floods and failed harvests were "promised action.".

    "They cannot survive on an annual renewal of promises," Adow mentioned.

    Industry observers note that he laid the blame squarely with the world's most developed nations: "They demand action from developing countries, then block public finance, block Just Transition, block climate finance, and they expect ambition. You cannot keep your foot on the brake and complain that countries are not moving fast enough.".

    Xiye Bastida, a Fresh York-based youth activist from Mexico, spoke to DW's Katharina Schantz to describe her frustration over the lack of progress and ambition on display at this year's COP Summit, which is the seventh the 24-year-old has attended.

    Bastida, who has played a leading role in the Fridays for Future climate movement in Upcoming York, mentioned she did not think she "could be more disappointed" at how climate targets are "being rolled back.".

    "This is really the time of reckoning," Bastida noted.

    She explained that she had changed her flight aims to be able to stay until the end, because she feels "we have to be here. We at least to be witnesses of how they're taking things away.".

    Bastida pointed to the hypocrisy from wealthy nations, who have blamed some from the Global South for not wanting the summit's joint declaration to mention fossil fuels.

    "But they (the Global North) are the ones not bringing the money, and they're the ones who are not bringing the ambition.

    According to recent reports, "And they want to show themselves as the leaders. But if you want to mention fossil fuels so bad, where's the money for the transition? Where are the roadmaps?

    "Are you serious?" Bastida concluded.

    The fresh draft declaration, which, as we've reported, has been panned by the EU and civil society, has also disappointed some of the world's least developed countries (LDCs) that are most vulnerable to climate change.

    The LDC Group, which comprises 44 of the world's least wealthy nations, came into this year's COP summit hoping for stronger climate action than what has been achieved so far.

    "It’s a moment of anticipation," Lamin Sheriff, a press attache for the Sierra Leone government, told DW's Katharina Schantz.

    "Ministers from LDCs have requests on the table for the presidency. So whilst they wait on what the outcome would be, everybody is waiting patiently. So the moment is really: we are hopeful for the future, but we are also worried because if proper care is not taken, all what we have debated about here in the last couple of weeks will just be a talk show (…) We can't do anything at the moment.".

    Caribbean nations fear economic impact of shuttering citizenship program after EU threats

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (670 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • St Kitts and Nevis to wind down citizenship-by-investment program after EU warns of end to visa-free access.
    • The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned.
    • On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, declared he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    St Kitts and Nevis to wind down citizenship-by-investment program after EU warns of end to visa-free access.

    The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned.

    On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, declared he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis.

    Mark Brantley, the premier of Nevis, which has autonomous self-governance in some aspects, stated he understood that the “country was given very little choice”, but did not “support the winding down of the program”.

    The 42-year-old CBI programme, which St Kitts and Nevis pioneered, allows wealthy foreigners to obtain citizenship and ultimately a passport by investing in infrastructure and other development projects. It has brought billions of dollars into the country and in some years accounted for the largest share of government revenue.

    Sources indicate that in June, the European Commission wrote to the five Caribbean nations that currently operate CBI programmes: St Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and St Lucia. It warned that countries may lose visa-free access to its 29-country Schengen area if they did not phase out CBI.

    In Friday’s statement, Drew blamed concerns over the programme on mismanagement by previous administrations, including years of underselling to undercut other countries, a controversial prison project, weak escrow protections and investment sums not being properly paid into the citizenship unit.

    He said his government had led major reforms to the Caribbean’s programmes with international partners, including the US treasury, but argued that continuing the programme risked visa-free travel to parts of Europe and access to international banking. That could disrupt services allowing visitors to use overseas cards and families abroad to send money home.

    Brantley, however, argued it was unfair for the EU to force St Kitts and Nevis to make a move without offering assistance to navigate the transition to other industries.

    Industry observers note that “I have not yet seen from the EU any corresponding suggestions of assistance. And we have to realise that these citizenship-by-investment programs, not only in St Kitts and Nevis, but … smaller countries of the Caribbean, have contributed significantly to our gross domestic product and also to ensuring that our people … can get adequate access to water and to education, to healthcare and the like,” he said.

    Brantley described the 1 June 2028 deadline the EU gave the country to phase out the lucrative programme as “frankly ludicrous”.

    In his statement, Drew said the CBI programme “did a lot of good, but it also created a danger”.

    Recent findings suggest that “When one source pays for half or more of everything, you are at its mercy. If it stops, everything stops. That is putting all of your eggs in one basket,” he added.

    It has been revealed that the prime minister said the government aimed to diversify its economy by strengthening tourism, yachting, and digital and creative industries, among others. He added that the sale of clean, geothermal energy was “at the heart of it” with drilling and exploration already planned.

    In a recent development, “I will not pretend that the road is easy. Less CBI money means we must spend wisely and strategy carefully. We will. Our plan is to make this change by growing our economy. Raising taxes is not part of that plan,” Drew said.

    Recent findings suggest that antigua and Barbuda has also expressed willingness to end the programme, though it is trying to negotiate a longer transition period. The five Caribbean governments have taken differing positions on the EU demand. According to local media, Grenada has indicated it wants its programme to continue until 2032, while Dominica and St Lucia have responded to Brussels without publicly committing to ending their programmes.

    Jermine Abel in Basseterre contributed reporting.

    When reached for comment by TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson didn’t deny the claims, merely providing the following statement: “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.”.

    So far, Meta has made a relatively successful push into consumer AI, launching Muse — its agentic helper — along with a variety of cute avatars that people can use to give the system more of a personality.

    Muse Charm, the manufacturer’s push into AI hardware, will allow consumers to carry a physical personification of its software around in their pocket (or potentially wear it around their neck), talking to it, asking it questions, and giving it commands.

    Sources indicate that it remains to be seen whether customers will bite or not. AI wearables have had a rough go of it so far (here’s looking at you, Humane Ai pin), but companies continue to iterate on the concept in an attempt to break through to a broader audience.

    Indeed, $300 is arguably a pretty steep price for a product the size of a keychain, although it’s also a price point that’s in line with what other companies have been charging. The wearable rolled out by Friend — the AI startup whose device lets you text and talk to an AI persona — is right now retailing for $250. On the other hand, Amazon’s all-fresh Bee Frontier wearable AI device — which transcribes conversations and tracks tasks — lists for $75 and is currently on a Black Friday, 30% off sale of $52.49. Even with its $99/year subscription to let it tie into a user’s apps (photos, emails, etc.), it’s still far less expensive than Muse Charm.
